newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban fire 65 men for trimming their beards.
newsitem.headline: Taleban fire 65 men for trimming their beards.

text.p: Afghanistan's purist Islamic Taleban movement has fired 65 government employees for trimming their beards, which are viewed by Moslems as a symbol of piety, a Taleban official said on Monday.

"We have told the people repeatedly to abide by Islamic law and not to trim their beards. We received an order from the Amir al-Momineen (Leader of the Faithful) to dismiss those who did not obey," said Maulawi Rafiullah Muazin, president of the department for Promoting Virtue and Preventing Vice.
"Leader of the Faithful" refers to Mullah Mohammed Omar, the head of the Taleban movement.
Muazin said the dismissals on Sunday were the largest to date, and that no one in government was exempt from the regulations.

"This is the first time such a large number of people have been dismissed. It does not matter who the person is, if he has trimmed his beard, we will dismiss him. We will never count the cost, God will carry our work forward," Muazin said.
Muazin explained to journalists that beards should be a certain length.
"The beards must be long enough to come out of a clenched fist held at the base of the chin, according to Islamic practice," said Muazin.
He said the Taleban programme of Islamic purification would continue.
"This is part of a wider programme and it will continue. We have departments in all provinces and we have ordered them to follow the programme," he said.
The Taleban, which seized Kabul last September and now control more than 75 percent of Afghanistan, have issued a number of edicts in their drive to create a pure Islamic state.
They have ordered women to wear a traditional Afghan veil that covers the face, banned women from schools and the work place and punish violators with whippings.

They have outlawed New Year celebrations, music, dancing, photographs, paper bags, and recently ordered residents of Kabul to paint over windows on upper floors to prevent them looking into their neighbour's yards.

Afghan-watchers say many of the regulations have as much to do with the culture of southern Afghanistan -- the birthplace of most of the Taleban leadership -- as with a strict interpretation of Islamic law.
